title: Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.

context.text: Placed on the ballot by petition signatures (citizen initiative), per the Official Voter Information Guide. The higher rates were first approved by voters in 2012 (Proposition 30) and extended in 2016.

question.text: PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT. Makes permanent the existing 2012 voter-approved tax rates for high-income Californians, currently set to expire in 2031. Rates apply to income over about $371,000 for single filers, $742,000 for joint filers, and $505,000 for heads of household (2025 levels; adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues 89% to K–12 schools, 11% to community colleges. Allows local school boards to decide how revenues are spent; bars use for administrative costs. Increases General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves, and other programs.

summary.text: Makes the higher personal income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Revenues go 89% to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges (local boards decide use; no administrative costs), and increases General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves, and other programs. Fiscal impact per the Legislative Analyst: brings in between $5 billion and $15 billion each year; roughly 40 percent would go to schools and community colleges and the rest to other state programs, part of it into budget reserves.

measure.yesMeans: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
measure.noMeans: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.

argumentsFor.text: Official argument in favor, signed by David Goldberg (California Teachers Association), Katie Nilsson, RN (California School Nurses Organization) and Jodi Hicks (Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California): "Proposition 3 is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone. Prop. 3 prevents millionaires and billionaires from getting a tax cut, and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms."
Same argument: "Without Prop. 3, California's 8 million public school and community college students face billions in cuts, including teacher layoffs, overcrowded classrooms and bigger class sizes."

argumentsAgainst.text: Official argument against, signed by Robert Gutierrez (California Taxpayers Association), Robert Rivinius (Family Business Association of California) and Julian Canete (California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce): "Politicians told voters higher income taxes would be temporary—only for seven years to cover a budget deficit." It adds: "Now the special interests and politicians want to make these higher income taxes PERMANENT."

Rebuttal to the argument in favor, signed by Jon Coupal (Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association), Carlos Solorzano (Hispanic Chambers of Commerce of San Francisco) and Clint Olivier (Central Valley Business Federation): "California doesn’t have a tax revenue problem—it has a spending problem." It also says the measure would be "costing taxpayers up to $15 billion every year."

currentLaw.text: Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily raise income tax rates on high-income taxpayers and Proposition 55 in 2016 to extend the higher rates until 2030 (the Analyst's proposal section refers to expiration in 2031). The top 2 percent of taxpayers pay these rates and about half of all state income taxes. Income tax pays for most General Fund spending, about half of which goes to schools, community colleges and universities.

fiscalImpact.text: Legislative Analyst: Proposition 3 would bring in between $5 billion and $15 billion each year (about $5 billion in a weak year, $15 billion in a strong year), varying with the stock market. Roughly 40 percent would go to schools and community colleges and the rest to other state programs, part set aside in budget reserves.

supporters.text: Yes on Prop 3 committees registered with the Secretary of State, including Yes on Prop 3 to Protect Public Education, Health Care and Budget Stability (sponsored by education and labor organizations).
California Teachers Association, California Federation of Teachers and California School Employees Association (named in the official argument in favor and/or signing the argument or rebuttal).

California State PTA, California Nurses Association, California School Nurses Organization, Community College League of California, Nurse Alliance of SEIU California and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California (listed in the official argument in favor).
California Professional Firefighters (signer of the rebuttal to the argument against).
California Democratic Party and California Medical Association (listed in CalMatters' voter guide).

opponents.text: California Taxpayers Association (President Robert Gutierrez; also sponsor of the No on Proposition 3 committee), Family Business Association of California and California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, signers of the official argument against.
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (Jon Coupal), Hispanic Chambers of Commerce of San Francisco and Central Valley Business Federation, signers of the rebuttal to the argument in favor.
Reform California (listed in CalMatters' voter guide).

campaignFinance.text: Support: $46,260,006 reported by four committees (Yes on Prop 3 to Protect Public Education, Health Care and Budget Stability, $44,174,753; Communities for an Affordable California, $1,090,000; Tax the Ultra-Rich Now, $703,494; Working Families for a Better Central Coast, $291,759); several of these committees also take positions on other measures (Props 39, 40, 41, 42, 43). Opposition: $5,500 reported by No on Proposition 3, sponsored by California Taxpayers Association. Source: Cal-Access totals as compiled by the Secretary of State from specified reports, through 10/06/2026.
